name: Sandakphu & the Singalila Ridge
tagline: Walk the border ridge to see Everest
meta_description: Sandakphu and the Singalila Ridge on a budget: lodge treks and old Land Rovers to West Bengal's highest point, with real costs, permits and seasons.
summary: The Singalila Ridge runs north along the India–Nepal border west of Darjeeling. From Maneybhanjan a trail and an old jeep track climb to Sandakphu (3,636 m), the highest point in West Bengal, where Everest, Kanchenjunga, Lhotse and Makalu share one horizon. Lodges, trekkers' huts and a licensed guide keep it affordable.

story.title: A border ridge, a poison hill and forty old jeeps
paras: The ridge you walk was bought. In 1882 the British government purchased the Singalila tract from the Sikkim Durbar and notified it as reserve forest, which is why the slopes above Maneybhanjan are still oak, rhododendron and silver fir instead of tea. Thirty-four years earlier the botanist Joseph Dalton Hooker had come up Tonglu from Darjeeling, collecting the rhododendrons that later filled British gardens. In 1905 the first documented attempt on Kanchenjunga, led by Jules Jacot-Guillarmod with Aleister Crowley in the party, marched north along this same ridge.

The highest top carries a warning in its name. Sandakphu is usually traced to Lepcha words for 'height of the poisonous plant', after the aconite (Aconitum ferox) and certain rhododendrons that once grew thick near the summit. Herders are said to have muzzled sheep and cattle driven across it so they could not graze. A little south, the col of Bikheybhanjang carries the same idea in Nepali: bikh means poison.

Today the ridge is a working frontier and a protected forest at once. Singalila became a wildlife sanctuary in 1986 and a national park in 1992, and red pandas still live in its bamboo and fir. The border with Nepal follows the crest, so the trail steps in and out of Ilam district at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri. And up the cobbled track grind the Land Rovers of Maneybhanjan, a fleet of 1950s and 1960s Series vehicles that still do the school, ration and trekker runs.

intro: Singalila is the cheapest high Himalayan view in India that you can reach without a permit office in a capital city. Shared jeeps from Darjeeling reach Maneybhanjan in about an hour. From there you either walk for three to four days up the ridge to Sandakphu, or hire one of the old Land Rovers that make the same climb in about four hours. Either way, the reward is the same: on a clear October morning the Kanchenjunga massif fills the north and Everest, Lhotse and Makalu stand to the west.

This is a lodge trek, not a camping trek. Tumling, Tonglu, Gairibas, Kalipokhri, Sandakphu and Phalut all have trekkers' huts or family lodges serving dal-bhat, noodle soup and tea. You carry a light pack and pay as you go. Beyond Sandakphu the trail runs 21 km along the ridge to Phalut at the Sikkim tri-junction, then drops through river villages, Gorkhey, Samanden, Rammam and Srikhola, to the jeep head at Rimbik.

Two rules shape every trip. Inside Singalila National Park a licensed local guide is compulsory and you pay park entry at Maneybhanjan. And the park closes for the monsoon, usually from mid-June to mid-September. Plan around both and Singalila is one of the best-value treks in the Himalaya, with lodge nights from a few hundred rupees and a guide whose daily fee is shared by the group.

highlights.title: Four of the five highest peaks
highlights.text: From Sandakphu on a clear morning you see Everest, Lhotse and Makalu to the west and the whole Kanchenjunga massif to the north. K2, the only one missing, is in the Karakoram. Few viewpoints anywhere put four 8,000-metre peaks in one sweep.

highlights.title: The Sleeping Buddha skyline
highlights.text: Kanchenjunga and its neighbouring summits form a long outline that guides call the Sleeping Buddha, a reclining figure with the main peak as the face. It is clearest at sunrise from Sandakphu, Tumling and Phalut, when the snow turns pink before the valleys clear.

highlights.title: The Land Rovers of Maneybhanjan
highlights.text: Around forty Land Rover Series vehicles, many from the 1950s and 1960s, run the cobbled track from Maneybhanjan to Sandakphu. The owners' association keeps them alive with patient mechanics. A ride is about four hours of bouncing, and the cheapest way up for anyone who cannot walk it.

highlights.title: Red panda country
highlights.text: Singalila National Park, 78.6 km² of oak, bamboo, rhododendron and silver fir, is one of the better places in India to see a wild red panda. Your chances are best in the quiet forest around Gairibas and Kalipokhri, early in the morning, from late autumn to spring.

highlights.title: Rhododendron months
highlights.text: From late March to May the ridge flowers in layers: red tree rhododendrons around Chitrey and Tonglu first, then pinks, whites and yellows higher up toward Sandakphu and Phalut. Hooker collected here in 1848. Views are hazier in these months, so you trade some mountains for flowers.

highlights.title: River villages on the way down
highlights.text: North of Sandakphu the trail leaves the crest and drops to Gorkhey, Samanden, Rammam and Srikhola, farm villages on cold rivers where you sleep in family lodges. Few trekkers go this far, which makes the last two days the quietest and often the warmest of the trip.

getting_there: Fly to Bagdogra or take a train to New Jalpaiguri (NJP), then go up to Darjeeling or Mirik. Shared jeeps from the Siliguri and NJP stands to Darjeeling cost about ₹250–350 a seat and take 3–3.5 hours. From Darjeeling's Chowk Bazaar motor stand, shared jeeps to Maneybhanjan run through the morning via Ghoom and Sukhiapokhri: ≈ 26 km, 1–1.5 hours, about ₹100–150 a seat. A reserved car from Darjeeling costs about ₹1,500–2,000; from NJP or Bagdogra straight to Maneybhanjan expect ₹3,500–4,500 for 3.5–4 hours. Coming out at Rimbik, shared jeeps leave early morning for Darjeeling (≈ 56 km, 4–5 hours, ₹200–300 a seat). Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.
permits: Singalila National Park needs an entry ticket and a licensed local guide for every group, whether you walk or ride a Land Rover. Both are arranged at the guide and park offices at Maneybhanjan; fees are indicative at about ₹100–200 per Indian adult, more for foreigners, plus a camera fee. The trail crosses into Nepal at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri, and SSB and Nepal police may check papers: Indians carry a passport or voter ID, foreigners carry a passport with a valid Indian visa. The park usually closes mid-June to mid-September. Check current status before you travel.
money: A walking trekker in a group of two who sleeps in dorms or basic lodge rooms spends roughly ₹2,000–2,500 a day: about ₹400–600 for a bed, ₹700–1,000 for three lodge meals and tea, and half of a ₹1,500–2,000 daily guide fee. A private twin room, a porter (₹1,000–1,300 a day) and bottled drinks push it to ₹3,000–4,000. The big single cost is a Land Rover: about ₹6,500–9,000 a vehicle for a Sandakphu round trip with a night, so it pays to fill all six seats. People overspend on reserved cars from NJP and on bottled water; carry a filter bottle instead. All prices are indicative.

months.weather: Sandakphu −8 to 4 °C, snow likely, very clear
months.summary: January is the cold, clear month. Snow often lies on the ridge above Tonglu and can block the Land Rover track for days at a time, but on the mornings it is open the views are the sharpest of the year. Lodges stay open with fewer guests and wood stoves in the dining rooms. You need proper down, gloves and boots with grip, and a guide who knows which stretches ice over.
months.tip: Ask at Maneybhanjan whether the track above Kalipokhri is passable before you hire a Land Rover.

months.summary: February brings the heaviest snowfalls in many years, and also Losar in Sherpa and Tamang homes in Rimbik and Maneybhanjan. Trekking is possible but slower, and you should carry a day's margin for weather. When it clears, the snowline sits low and the Sleeping Buddha looks enormous. Few trekkers means quiet huts and easy beds without booking.
months.tip: Pack microspikes; they cost little in Darjeeling and save a lot of falls.

months.summary: March is the shoulder month. Snow retreats from the lower ridge, the first red rhododendrons open around Chitrey and Tonglu, and haze starts to build in the afternoons. Mornings are still often clear. It is a good month for a quieter trek to Sandakphu with a fair chance of mountains and early flowers, and lodge rooms are easy to find.
months.tip: Start walking by 7 am; afternoon cloud now comes up from the valleys most days.

months.summary: April is rhododendron month. The red, pink and white trees flower in bands from Tonglu up to Sandakphu, and magnolias show in the forest around Gairibas. Views are hazier than in autumn, though dawn often still shows Kanchenjunga. This is busy season with Indian families and student groups, so book trekkers' huts or a lodge room ahead for weekends.
months.tip: The best flowering moves uphill through the month: lower ridge early April, Phalut side by early May.

months.summary: Early May keeps the high rhododendrons and the long days; late May brings pre-monsoon storms most afternoons and thick haze. Mountain views become a matter of luck at dawn. It is still pleasant walking weather, warmer than any other open month, and the river villages below Phalut are green and lively with farm work.
months.tip: Plan the long Sandakphu to Phalut day for the morning; storms usually build after 1 pm.

months.summary: The national park usually closes to trekkers from mid-June to mid-September, and the first half of June is wet, cloudy and leech-heavy anyway. The Land Rover track turns to mud. Maneybhanjan itself stays reachable by road, but there is no good reason to plan a Singalila trek now. Visit Darjeeling instead and come back in October.
months.tip: Check current status before you travel; closure dates are set by the forest department.

months.summary: July is peak monsoon on the ridge, with rain most days, landslides on the access roads and the park closed to trekkers. The villages below, like Rimbik, live quietly through the rains; roads from Darjeeling can be cut for days. We do not recommend travel to Singalila in July.
months.tip: If you are in Darjeeling, the Singalila forest is better seen from the Ghoom side this month.

months.summary: August is the same story: heavy rain, cloud on the ridge and the park closed. Hillside roads to Rimbik and Dhotrey slip in places. The upside is that the forest is at its greenest when the park reopens. Use August to plan and book October huts and lodges.
months.tip: October weekends and the Puja holidays fill up; book in August.

months.summary: The park usually reopens around mid-September, but the second half of the month is still damp, with cloud most afternoons and the odd clear dawn. Trails are muddy and leeches linger below 2,500 m. If your dates are fixed, the last week of September can work for a short trip to Tumling or Tonglu.
months.tip: Carry salt or leech socks for the forest below Chitrey and Dhotrey.

months.summary: October is the classic month. The monsoon has washed the air, mornings are clear and the whole skyline from Everest to Kanchenjunga stands out sharply. Dashain and Tihar fall in October or early November, filling villages with swings, flowers and family visits. It is also the busiest time on the ridge, with Puja holiday crowds, so book huts and Land Rovers early.
months.tip: Avoid the main Puja holiday week if you want quiet lodges.

months.weather: Sandakphu −2 to 9 °C, very clear, cold nights
months.summary: November is our favourite month: settled, dry, clear and colder, with frost on the huts and the best visibility of the year. Crowds thin after the Puja holidays. Nights at Sandakphu drop below freezing, so carry a proper sleeping bag or ask for extra blankets. It is the best time for the full trek to Phalut and down to Rimbik.
months.tip: Watch sunset from Sandakphu as well as sunrise; the light on Makalu is often better in the evening.

months.summary: December stays clear and turns properly cold, with the first snow often arriving late in the month. The ridge is quieter except over Christmas and New Year, when Kolkata families come for snow. Views are excellent. Plan short trekking days, as the light goes by about 4.45 pm, and carry warm layers for the lodge dining rooms.
months.tip: Over Christmas and New Year, book the Land Rover and lodge together, a week ahead.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory for the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Inside Singalila National Park every group must take a licensed local guide, arranged at the guide office in Maneybhanjan. The fee is per group per day, indicatively ₹1,500–2,000, so it is far cheaper per head in a group of four than for a solo walker. The rule applies to Land Rover trips too. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do you need for Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Walking up from Maneybhanjan and down to Rimbik via Srikhola takes four to five days. Adding Phalut and the river villages makes it seven to eight days. By Land Rover you can reach Sandakphu in about four hours and be back in Maneybhanjan the next morning, so two nights from Darjeeling is the minimum sensible plan.

faqs.q: Can you see Everest from Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. Everest, Lhotse and Makalu appear to the west, roughly 125–145 km away, alongside Kanchenjunga about 70 km to the north. Visibility is best from October to December, usually at dawn before cloud builds. In April and May haze often hides the western peaks even when Kanchenjunga shows.

faqs.q: Do you need a passport to trek to Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Indians do not need a passport, but should carry a passport or voter ID because the trail passes through Nepal at Tumling, Jaubari and Kalipokhri, and Aadhaar alone may not be accepted. Foreign trekkers must carry their passport with a valid Indian visa for SSB and police checks. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does the Sandakphu trek cost?
faqs.a: A budget walker in a pair spends roughly ₹2,000–2,500 a day on beds, meals and a half share of the guide. A full five-night trek from NJP and back, with shared jeeps and basic lodges, comes to about ₹12,000–14,000 per person. A Land Rover trip with private rooms costs ₹13,000–15,000 per person for two nights. All prices are indicative.

faqs.q: When does Singalila National Park close?
faqs.a: The park usually closes to tourists for the monsoon from mid-June to mid-September, a rule set by the West Bengal forest department to protect trails and wildlife during the rains. Exact dates can shift, and heavy snow can also shut the Land Rover track in January and February. Check current status before you travel.

It is a moderate trek. Days are 6–21 km on rough paths and cobbled track, with the steepest climbs from Maneybhanjan to Chitrey and from Kalipokhri to Sandakphu. The altitude, up to 3,636 m, is enough to cause headaches, so ascend steadily and drink water. Fit beginners manage it with a guide and a light pack.

faqs.q: Where do you stay on the Singalila trek?
faqs.a: In trekkers' huts run by the GTA and in small family lodges at Tumling, Tonglu, Gairibas, Kalipokhri, Sandakphu and Phalut, then in village lodges at Gorkhey, Rammam and Srikhola. Expect dorm beds or basic twin rooms, shared toilets, thick quilts and a dining room with a stove. Hot water usually costs extra.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Patchy. Indian networks reach Maneybhanjan and parts of Tumling and Sandakphu, but much of the ridge picks up Nepali networks, which can trigger roaming charges. Expect no signal in the forest around Gairibas and in the river villages. Lodges sometimes have Wi-Fi when the power is on. Tell family you may be unreachable for a day or two.
